strengths: Novel and well-motivated framework (RL-D2) that fills a genuine gap: principled online RL training of discrete (masked) diffusion policies for combinatorial action spaces, framing policy improvement as distribution matching to a PMD target.

The two variants (forward-KL weighted ELBO / self-imitation style loss and reverse-KL with PPO-style clipped single-step ratios) are derived with supporting proofs in the appendix (B.1–B.3), and the connection to classification-based policy iteration (Remark 1) is a nice conceptual link.

Unusually broad empirical evaluation across three very different domains: DNA enhancer generation (vs. CG, SMC, TDS, CFG, DRAKES), macro-action RL on MinAtar and the full 56-game Atari benchmark (vs. DQN, IMPALA, R2D2, PPO and macro variants), and cooperative MARL on Google Research Football (11 vs 11 included).

Useful practical analyses beyond headline results: computational/memory savings vs. DRAKES (66.4GB→10.6GB), inference-time efficiency with few diffusion steps, top-p sampling and remasking for long macro-actions, and ablations of temperature auto-tuning, on-policy diffusion learning, architecture (MLP vs transformer), and a planner variant exploiting non-causal unmasking.
The on-policy diffusion learning idea (Sec. 4.2) of sampling the full reverse trajectory to align training and inference distributions is a sensible and ablation-supported contribution.
Computationally efficient alternative to backpropagating rewards through the full reverse process, addressing a real scalability bottleneck of prior discrete-diffusion fine-tuning methods.
weaknesses: Presentation quality is below bar for a main-track submission: multiple typos and grammatical errors ('this ration', 'don't need', 'confidential intervals', 'we don't need to change the ELBO ... We only need to change' — an incomplete sentence in App. C.3), a broken citation '()zekri2025fine', Figure 10's caption is a copy-paste error from Figure 9 (describes on-policy ablation, not architecture), Figure 8's caption is truncated, and Table 4 lists 'Discount factor' twice.

Statistical rigor is thin for RL claims: only 3 random seeds with 95% CIs on highly variable Atari results, and several huge score values (e.g., Breakout 20.18K, Space Invaders 178.9K in Table 1; Berzerk 802.99K in Table 5) are far above typical magnitudes and are not explained — whether macro-action length changes score accounting or evaluation protocol needs clarification to rule out evaluation artifacts.

Theoretical guarantees are weaker than the framing suggests: the forward-KL result is a one-sided ELBO-based bound on the KL, the ELBO-difference importance ratio is acknowledged as biased, and the single-step ratio assumes the augmented-MDP advantage construction; no analysis of the accumulated approximation error or when the update preserves the PMD improvement property.

Baselines in each domain are somewhat limited and not always the strongest available: DIME and other discrete-diffusion RL/fine-tuning methods are cited but not compared; in Atari, no diffusion-based or stronger macro-action baseline is included; and the diffusion policy uses a larger/different architecture (transformer with FiLM conditioning on top of the shared CNN+LSTM), raising compute-fairness questions despite the scaling discussion.

The choice of FKL vs. RKL per domain is made post hoc (FKL for DNA/Atari, RKL for football) without a head-to-head comparison of both objectives on a common benchmark, weakening the claimed analysis of the two divergences.

No code release or clear reproducibility statement, and no limitations section discussing the horizon-complexity failure regime (performance peaks at macro length 4 with fixed budget, Fig. 3 left), sensitivity of the FKL partition-function estimator to the number of sampled actions, or inference cost of multi-step denoising at decision time.

Several reported wins are narrow: on MinAtar the method loses to DQN on Asterix and to DQN-Macro on Seaquest; on Atari the aggregate advantage in Fig. 2 is modest relative to the added complexity, and the paper's 'state-of-the-art' claim rests on comparisons within each of the three specific setups.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: training discrete diffusion policies for large combinatorial action spaces is an underexplored direction, and the PMD-based 'distribution matching' framing (fitting the diffusion model to the analytic mirror-descent target) is a clean and sensible design that decouples RL optimization from representation learning.

Deriving both forward-KL and reverse-KL variants of the policy improvement step, with connections to self-imitation/classification-based policy iteration (Appendix B), gives the method a reasonable conceptual grounding and offers practitioners a mean-seeking vs. mode-seeking choice.

The evaluation scope is ambitious and spans three genuinely different domains (DNA reward-guided generation, macro-action Atari/MinAtar, cooperative MARL in Google Research Football), plus useful practical contributions such as on-policy diffusion training, temperature auto-tuning via a hard KL constraint (Appendix C.2), and inference-time techniques (top-p, remasking).
Demonstrated efficiency gains over DRAKES on the DNA task (reduced GPU memory from 66.4 GB to 10.6 GB and time from 268 to 97 minutes) are concrete and valuable.

Several ablations are provided (temperature tuning, on-policy diffusion learning, architecture choice, diffusion-as-planner), and scalability analysis over macro-action length is a relevant question for this problem class.
weaknesses: Serious soundness concerns in the headline MinAtar results (Table 1): scores of 20.18K on Breakout and 178.9K on Space Invaders are orders of magnitude beyond any scores reported in the MinAtar literature, suggesting a nonstandard or buggy evaluation protocol that is never explained. Moreover, the claim of winning '4 out of 5 tasks' does not hold against the table itself (RL-D2 loses to DQN on Asterix and to DQN-Macro on Seaquest, and Freeway is within noise), which undermines confidence in the empirical reporting.

Statistical support is thin: only 3 random seeds for the Atari/MinAtar experiments, and Table 2 reports 'maximum mean win rate,' a selection-biased metric that overstates performance; several Football scenario gains (e.g., 75.4 vs 95 on ct-easy) are actually losses but the text claims superiority 'in almost every scenario.'

Baseline coverage is incomplete for the SOTA claims: the MARL comparison includes only an autoregressive transformer, omitting standard cooperative MARL baselines (e.g., MAPPO, QMIX variants); Atari baselines, while decent, are not tuned for the macro-action setting comparably to the proposed method, and no discrete-diffusion RL competitor is included beyond DRAKES in one domain.

Theoretical treatment is informal where it matters most: the FKL objective is only a bound on the forward KL after approximating Z(s) from sampled actions, the ELBO-based importance ratio is acknowledged as biased but the bias is never quantified or empirically measured, and the 'on-policy diffusion learning' proposal in Sec. 4.2 is heuristic without analysis of when sampling the full reverse trajectory helps or hurts.

Writing and editorial quality are below the bar for a main-track submission: a broken citation '( )zekri2025fine' in Sec. 2, 'confidential intervals' for confidence intervals (multiple places), 'this ration', 'don't need', 'Mode Architechtures', 'outperm', duplicated reference entries (Sohl-Dickstein 2015 twice; Tomar 2020/2021; Wen et al. 2022a/b), and Table 4 lists 'Discount factor' twice with different values (0.995 vs 0.999), leaving the true setting ambiguous.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed: hyperparameters are given, but there is no mention of code release, and key evaluation details (e.g., how the anomalous MinAtar scores were computed) are missing, making independent verification difficult.

A limitations discussion and broader-impact/ethics note are absent, which is particularly noticeable given the DNA-sequence design application where reward over-optimization has real-world implications.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated framework: framing the policy improvement step of discrete diffusion policies as distribution matching to a PMD-derived target is a clean and principled idea, and the separation of RL optimization from representation learning is a sensible design choice.

Derives both forward-KL (weighted ELBO / self-imitation style) and reverse-KL (PPO-style with a tractable single-step importance ratio) variants, with derivations in the appendix (Appendix B) connecting the losses to PMD and to classification-based policy iteration.

Broad empirical scope across three genuinely different domains (DNA reward-guided generation, macro-action Atari/MinAtar, cooperative Google Research Football), which is more diverse than typical diffusion-policy papers.

Demonstrates concrete practical advantages: large reductions in GPU memory (66.4 GB to 10.6 GB) and compute time vs. DRAKES on DNA generation, inference-time efficiency with few diffusion steps (Fig. 1 right, Fig. 5), and useful ablations (temperature auto-tuning via hard KL constraint, on-policy diffusion training, planner variant, architecture).
The duality-based temperature tuning scheme (Appendix C.2) is a nice practical contribution applicable to both discrete and continuous diffusion RL.
weaknesses: The headline empirical claim of the macro-action experiments is inconsistent with the paper's own Table 1: the text claims 'substantially stronger performance in 4 out of 5 tasks' on MinAtar, but RL-D2 clearly loses to DQN on Asterix (50.37 vs 276.10) and to DQN-Macro on Seaquest (161.0 vs 171.80), and only marginally wins Freeway. This misrepresentation of results undermines trust in the empirical analysis.

Several reported scores are implausible and unexplained, suggesting reward exploitation or bugs: Breakout at 20.18K (orders of magnitude beyond typical Atari scores of a few hundred) and Space Invaders at 178.9K, both with enormous variance (±64.63K). The paper does not discuss whether these reflect action repetition exploits of macro-actions, raising questions about what the 'superior performance' actually measures.

Evaluation rigor is thin: only 3 random seeds for MinAtar, and the full-Atari comparison (Fig. 2) is a single aggregate human-normalized score over 56 environments without per-game significance analysis in the main text; several environments show large regressions in Fig. 6 that are not discussed.

Theoretical treatment is loose where it matters most. The FKL objective minimizes an upper bound on the forward KL obtained by dropping the target entropy and applying the ELBO inequality; minimizing this bound is not guaranteed to reduce the actual KL, and no analysis of bound tightness is given. The ELBO-based importance ratio for RKL is acknowledged as biased, but the magnitude/impact of the bias is never analyzed.

The 'On-Policy Diffusion Learning' contribution (Sec. 4.2), presented as a core innovation, is supported by only a single ablation figure (Fig. 9) in the appendix; the claim that it 'enhances stability and sample efficiency' is under-evidenced.

Baseline coverage is incomplete in key comparisons: in MARL the only comparison is a single autoregressive transformer baseline (no CTDE methods like QMIX/MAPPO); DQN-Macro is arguably a strawman since outputting |A|^4 logits scales poorly by construction.

Significant presentation and quality-control issues: typos throughout ('ration', 'outputt', 'implemetned', 'don't need'), a broken/garbled citation URL (Wen et al. 2022a), duplicated bibliography entries (Tomar 2020/2021; Sohl-Dickstein 2015 twice; Wen et al. 2022a/b duplicated), an incomplete Figure 8 caption, and Table 4 listing 'Discount factor' twice with 'Diffusion steps: Num of players', which appears to be an error. These suggest the manuscript was not carefully proofread.

No explicit code release statement or limitations section; reproducibility for the distributed R2D2-style Atari implementation at this scale is a concern given the complexity of the setup and the anomalous scores.

strengths: Timely and relevant problem: the paper targets the underexplored intersection of online RL and discrete (masked) diffusion models for large combinatorial action spaces, and the PMD-based 'distributional matching' framing of the policy improvement step is a clean and sensible design that connects to established ideas (MPO, classification-based policy iteration).

Comprehensive and unusually broad empirical evaluation across three genuinely different domains: reward-guided DNA generation (with strong baselines like DRAKES, SMC, TDS, CFG), macro-action RL in MinAtar/Atari, and cooperative MARL in Google Research Football against MAT and MAPPO.

Considerable statistical care: stratified bootstrap confidence intervals with 50k iterations, IQM/median/mean reporting for Atari, 20 seeds on MinAtar and Football, and detailed hyperparameter and baseline-selection documentation in the appendix.

Honest and useful empirical analysis of the FKL vs. RKL trade-off (sample efficiency vs. asymptotic performance/stability), including failure modes of FKL under temperature misspecification, ablations of temperature tuning, on-policy diffusion training, architecture, and sampling techniques (top-p, remasking).

Practical efficiency wins are quantified: substantial reductions in GPU memory (66.4 GB to 10.6 GB) and runtime (268 to 97 minutes) relative to DRAKES, and inference-time efficiency vs. autoregressive generation with few diffusion steps.
The appendices contain the full derivations for the FKL bound and RKL equivalence to the PMD objective, plus a temperature autotuning scheme via hard KL constraints.
weaknesses: The theoretically grounded claims are weaker than the framing suggests: the practical FKL objective is a weighted ELBO lower bound where the PMD normalizer Z(s) is estimated by sampling only M actions from the old policy (Appendix B.1), and the quality/bias of this softmax-reweighted approximation is never analyzed or empirically validated. The RKL variant similarly inherits the high-variance augmented-MDP single-step ratio construction from Ren et al. (2024) rather than contributing new theory.

Some 'state-of-the-art' claims are overstated. On MinAtar, RL-D² is strongest in only 2 of 5 tasks and clearly loses to DQN on Asterix and Freeway. The extreme Atari results (e.g., Breakout 20.58K, Space Invaders 184.3K, Berzerk 802K) are attributed to 'staying alive for a very long time', but no qualitative analysis is given to rule out degenerate loop-exploiting policies rather than genuinely superior long-horizon strategies.

Atari comparisons rest on only 3 seeds per game, and several baseline numbers appear surprisingly weak relative to published results (e.g., R2D2 mean human-normalized score of 6.31), raising concerns about baseline tuning even though some hyperparameter search is documented (only for DQN-Macro).

Compute/parameter budgets between RL-D² and baselines are not fully equalized in all experiments; wall-time comparisons are addressed only in the FKL-vs-RKL study, and the scalability claims partially rely on scaling RL-D²'s model size and data while baselines are fixed or fail to train.

Presentation and reproducibility gaps: Table 4 contains duplicated 'Discount factor' rows and an empty value for 'Diffusion steps'; multiple typos ('Tempearture', 'leaning rate', 'RL−D³' vs. RL-D² in Appendix G); no explicit code release is stated, which limits reproducibility of a system with many interacting components (temperature schedules, on-policy diffusion training, replay setup).

The comparison against autoregressive joint-action modeling is only fully performed in the Football domain, and the naive AR baseline is weak; MAT mitigates the causal-ordering issue, so the central claim that non-causal diffusion generation is the key advantage would be strengthened by AR-with-alignment baselines in the Atari macro-action setting.

The paper lacks an explicit limitations discussion beyond the FKL/RKL trade-off; sensitivity of the framework to temperature schedules (documented collapse modes) is treated as a finding rather than acknowledged as a practical limitation requiring tuning guidance.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important problem—RL over large combinatorial action spaces—and covers three distinct, challenging domains (DNA sequence generation, Atari with macro-actions, Google Research Football), which gives unusually broad empirical coverage for this area.

The core idea is clearly articulated: use Policy Mirror Descent to construct an analytic target distribution and train a discrete diffusion policy to match it via FKL or RKL, decoupling representation learning from policy improvement. The FKL/RKL derivation (Appendix B) is correct and connects nicely to self-imitation/classification policy iteration (Remark 2).

The empirical analysis of the FKL vs. RKL trade-off (sample efficiency vs. asymptotic performance/stability, Sec. 5.4, Figs. 4, 13) is one of the more valuable contributions and offers practical guidance to practitioners.

Useful secondary contributions: the dual-based KL-constrained temperature auto-tuning (Appendix C.2), on-policy diffusion learning (Sec. 4.2, ablated in Fig. 15), and inference-time techniques (top-p, remasking) with timestep ablations.

Statistical treatment is above average for RL papers: stratified bootstrap confidence intervals with 50k iterations (Appendix D.5), per-game full results (Table 5), and difference-in-IQM/median plots (Fig. 9).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the framework is a combination of known components—masked discrete diffusion (Shi et al., 2024), PMD-derived targets as distribution-matching policy improvement (MPO, Abdolmaleki et al., 2018; Chan et al., 2022), the self-imitation/weighted-ELBO trick, and the single-step importance-sampling ratio for diffusion policies taken directly from Ren et al. (2024). The authors should more explicitly delineate which elements are new versus inherited; as written, the derivations are largely straightforward applications of prior work.

Comparison fairness in the macro-action experiments is questionable. In MinAtar (Table 1), RL-D2 posts scores like 20.58K on Breakout and 184.3K on Space Invaders—orders of magnitude above all baselines—which the text attributes to staying alive indefinitely. This suggests the macro-action framing changes the effective MDP (longer commitment horizons), making 'substantially stronger performance in 2 out of 5 tasks' a claim about the setup rather than clearly about the policy class. The main Atari aggregate (Fig. 3) compares against mostly single-action baselines (PPO, R2D2) rather than strong sequence-modeling or diffusion-based policies, and the very high mean human-normalized score (31 vs. 9–18) deserves more scrutiny and discussion of why it is so far beyond published state-of-the-art.

The headline 'state-of-the-art' claim is overreached relative to the evidence: on MinAtar the method wins clearly on only 2 of 5 games; on Football the metric is 'maximum mean win rate' over training, which inflates performance versus final or median performance; and the strong asymmetry in Table 2 (RKL scoring 0.0 in the small-budget 11 vs 11 setting while FKL reaches 68.5) shows high sensitivity to objective/configuration choices that is acknowledged only partially.

Theoretical guarantees are thin: FKL optimizes only an ELBO bound on the target KL, and the practical FKL loss further approximates the partition function by softmax over a sample of actions (Appendix B.1), so the connection between what is provably convergent (PMD) and what is actually optimized is loose. No convergence or policy-improvement analysis of the practical algorithms is provided.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned, results rely on only 3 seeds per Atari game (168 total runs), and several results are reported with suspicious zero variance (e.g., IMPALA Space Invaders 47.71 [47.71, 47.71], Table 5 Breakout 424.15 ± 0.00), suggesting possible evaluation pipeline issues that are not discussed.

Presentation and completeness issues: Table 4 contains duplicated/erroneous entries (Discount factor listed twice, 'Diffusion steps / Num of players / Ratio clip' rows mislabeled), typos ('Tempearture', 'Critic leaning rate'), no dedicated limitations section, and a boilerplate impact statement. The abstract oscillates between 'state-of-the-art' and 'comparable or superior' without clarity.

Missing important related baselines for the core claim: for combinatorial action spaces, learned macro-action discovery, options frameworks, or hierarchical policies with learned termination would be more appropriate competitors than naive DQN-Macro/IMPALA-Macro variants, particularly for the Atari experiments that anchor the strongest claims.

strengths: The core idea—training discrete diffusion policies by matching them to a Policy Mirror Descent (PMD) target via forward/reverse KL—is a well-motivated and timely contribution, and the paper appears to be among the first to apply online RL training to discrete diffusion policies for genuinely combinatorial action spaces.

The mathematical development is careful: Appendix B.1 derives the FKL weighted-ELBO objective from the forward KL to the PMD target, Appendix B.2 shows the RKL objective recovers the mirror-descent policy improvement step, and Appendix C.2 gives a duality-based temperature tuning scheme via hard KL constraints. Remark 2 connecting the λ→0 limit to classification policy iteration (Lazaric et al., 2016) is a nice touch.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad: DNA sequence generation (against CG, SMC, TDS, CFG, DRAKES), macro-action RL on MinAtar and 56 Atari games (against DQN, IMPALA, PPO, R2D2 and macro variants), and MARL on Google Research Football (against MAPPO, MAT). Reporting includes stratified bootstrap confidence intervals with IQM/median (Appendix D.5, Table 6), which exceeds common practice in RL papers.

The paper is commendably honest about the FKL vs. RKL trade-off (Sec. 5.4): FKL is sample-efficient but collapse-prone under poor temperature selection; RKL is slower but more stable with better asymptotic performance. Failure modes are shown explicitly (Figs. 11–13) rather than hidden.

Rich ablations: on-policy diffusion training, temperature/KL-constraint schedules, network architecture, sampling techniques (top-p, remasking), and an interesting 'diffusion-as-planner' variant exploiting non-causal unmasking (Appendix E.4). The compute-efficiency comparison to DRAKES (66.4→10.6 GB memory, 268→97 minutes) is practically meaningful.

The scalability analysis (Fig. 5, macro-action lengths 8/16 with proportionally scaled compute) directly addresses the central claim about combinatorial action spaces, showing baselines fail or degrade where the diffusion policy scales.
weaknesses: Over-claiming relative to the evidence. The contributions section claims 'In all settings, our method achieves state-of-the-art results,' but Table 1 shows mixed MinAtar results: DQN wins Asterix (284 vs 52) and roughly matches on Freeway/Seaquest, and RL-D² beats macro baselines decisively in only 2 of 5 MinAtar tasks. Similarly, RL-D²-RKL scores 0.0 win rate on the 11 vs 11 SM scenario (Table 2). The abstract's more hedged 'comparable or superior' is more accurate than the contributions text; claims should be calibrated.

Several theoretical gaps are unquantified. (i) The FKL loss is an ELBO-based lower bound on the KL objective—the tightness of this bound is never discussed or measured. (ii) The RKL 'augmented MDP' trick (following Ren et al., 2024) assigns the final clean-action advantage to every denoising step, which is a strong approximation whose induced bias is not analyzed or empirically isolated. (iii) There are no convergence guarantees for the full policy-iteration loop—only the improvement step is grounded in PMD theory.

Statistical strength is uneven across claims. The headline Atari comparison uses only 3 seeds per game (168 runs total), and the FKL-vs-RKL comparisons in Fig. 4 use 3 seeds; the temperature ablations in Figs. 12–15 similarly rest on small seed counts. In a high-variance domain like Atari, these are thin margins for the finer-grained conclusions drawn.

The DNA experiment is a single-step bandit with a single dataset and a single reward oracle family, so it validates reward-optimization but says little about sequential decision-making; its inclusion as evidence for 'RL' claims should be tempered. It also relies on the reward model of Wang et al. (2024a), raising the question of whether gains partly reflect oracle exploitation despite the held-out oracle design.

Baseline comparability concerns: in Atari, RL-D² uses an R2D2-style distributed system with transformer actor/critic heads and FiLM conditioning, while baselines use the shared CNN+LSTM backbone; the macro baselines (DQN-Macro outputting |A|^K logits, IMPALA-Macro factorized logits) are reasonable but fairly weak adaptations. The horizon-complexity 'scalability' result (Fig. 5 middle/right) grants RL-D² proportionally more model capacity, heads, batch size, samples, and wall-time than the baselines shown in the same figure, so the scalability comparison conflates method and budget.

Reproducibility is only partial. Hyperparameters are provided (Tables 3–4), but there is no explicit statement of code release. Table 4 also contains apparent errors (Discount factor listed twice, an ambiguous 'Diffusion steps / Num of players' row), and there are typos ('Tempearture', 'Critic leaning rate') that suggest the appendix was not carefully proofread. Some details central to stability (e.g., exact on-policy diffusion training procedure, how the replay buffer interacts with FKL off-policy claims) are described at a high level only.

The 'off-policy' advantage of FKL (Sec. 2, Appendix G) is asserted but never demonstrated: all reported FKL experiments appear to be on-policy; no offline-dataset or replay-heavy experiment substantiates this claim.

Related work comparisons are incomplete: recent discrete-diffusion RL/fine-tuning methods (e.g., DIME, Celik et al., 2025; Zekri & Boullé, 2025) are cited but not empirically compared, and the discussion of why PMD-target matching is preferable to direct score-entropy reward optimization is qualitative only.
